titleEn: Renovation Contract Vancouver 2026: What to Know Before Signing
titleZh: 溫哥華裝修合同2026：簽約前必須知道的事
contentEn:
A renovation contract is a written agreement between you and your contractor that specifies exactly what work will be done, at what price, and on what timeline. In Vancouver and across Metro Vancouver, BC law sets specific rules around deposits, licensing, and warranty that every homeowner must understand before signing — because once you commit, enforcing your rights becomes expensive and slow.

Why Vancouver Homeowners Need a Written Renovation Contract

Vancouver homeowners face unique conditions that make a written renovation contract especially important. The city has some of the oldest housing stock in Canada — many homes built before current building codes — combined with complex strata governance rules, hillside site logistics, and permit backlogs that can push timelines well beyond what contractors initially estimate. For strata buildings, BC's Strata Property Act requires written council approval before any renovation that affects common property, structural elements, or exterior appearance. Without a contract that references these approval processes, a contractor can legally begin work before your strata council has signed off.

BC's Homeowner Protection Act also mandates a 10-day cooling-off period after you sign a renovation contract and pay a deposit — a protection that exists precisely because renovation disputes are the single largest category of consumer complaints in the province. Use that 10 days to review, ask questions, and never rush a signature.

What Must Be in Every Vancouver Renovation Contract

A binding renovation contract in BC should include all of the following:

  • Full scope of work — a detailed written description of every task, material, and finish, with brand names or model numbers for key fixtures. Vague scopes like "renovate bathroom" create disputes later.
  • Complete price and payment schedule — the total contract price, deposit amount, and payment milestones tied to completed work stages. Avoid lump-sum contracts with no stage payments.
  • Timeline with milestones — start date, major stage completion dates (demolition, rough-in, finishing, final inspection), and an estimated completion date. Include consequences for missed milestones.
  • Change order procedure — any addition or modification to the original scope requires a written change order signed by both parties before extra work begins. Verbal authorizations are not binding.
  • Insurance requirements — minimum $2 million general liability coverage, and written proof of WorkSafeBC coverage for any workers on your property. Ask for certificates of insurance and verify directly with the insurer.
  • Permit responsibility — who applies for and pays for building permits, and what happens if a permit is denied or delayed.
  • Warranty terms — minimum 1-year labour warranty on all work, plus manufacturer warranties on installed products.

BC Licensing Requirements for Renovation Contractors

Under BC law, any renovation contractor performing work valued at more than $5,000 must hold a valid BC business licence and be registered as a residential builder with BC Housing. Licensed residential builders are legally required to provide new home warranty insurance on their work, covering structural defects and materials for a minimum period. Ask your contractor for their BC Housing registration number and verify it at the Homeowner Protection Online Portal. Hiring an unlicensed contractor in BC voids your warranty protections and may void your home insurance.

For work in strata buildings, confirm that your contractor has experience coordinating with strata councils — this is a skill separate from construction competence. Contractors unfamiliar with Form B requirements and strata approval processes routinely cause costly delays.

Deposit and Payment Protections for BC Homeowners

BC's Homeowner Protection Act limits deposits to a maximum of $5,000 or half the total contract price, whichever is less. If a contractor asks for more, that is a warning sign. On contracts over $1,000, BC law also mandates a minimum 5% holdback — money you retain and release only after the project passes final inspection. The holdback exists as your leverage if a contractor walks off the job or does substandard work.

Dispute Resolution and How to Protect Yourself

BC homeowners have two primary avenues for renovation disputes: the Residential Tenancy Authority for contracts under $50,000, and the BC Civil Resolution Tribunal for claims up to $5,000. For larger disputes or structural defects, BC courts are the remaining option — expensive and slow. Prevention is always better than cure: ensure your contract names a specific dispute resolution process before signing.

Watch for these red flags in any renovation contract offered to you: refusal to provide a detailed scope, demands for more than $5,000 deposit or full payment upfront, cash-only arrangements, no timeline or milestone schedule, resistance to providing insurance certificates, reluctance to apply for permits, and pressure to sign quickly.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the maximum deposit a contractor can ask for in BC?

Under BC's Homeowner Protection Act, a contractor can ask for a maximum deposit of $5,000 or half the total contract price, whichever is less. If a contractor demands more, you can refuse and report them to Consumer Protection BC.

Can I add changes to the scope after signing a renovation contract?

Yes — but only with a written change order signed by both you and the contractor before the extra work begins. Verbal authorizations are not legally binding and contractors are not obligated to honour them without a signed change order.

How do I verify a contractor is licensed in BC?

Search the Homeowner Protection Online Portal on the BC Housing website using the contractor's business name or registration number. Check that their licence is current and that their insurance coverage is active before signing.

Is there a cooling-off period for renovation contracts in BC?

Yes. BC's Homeowner Protection Act provides a 10-day cooling-off period for residential renovation contracts after signing and deposit payment. Use this period to review the contract thoroughly and consult a professional if needed.

Does my home insurance cover renovation work?

Standard home insurance does not cover faulty workmanship or incomplete work — it covers sudden and accidental damage. Ensure your contractor carries contractor's installation floater insurance for materials and workmanship during construction.

裝修合同是業主與承包商之間的書面協議，訂明工程內容、價格和工期。在溫哥華及大溫哥華地區，卑詩省法律對押金、執照和保修有特定規定，在簽約前必須了解清楚。

為什麼溫哥華業主需要書面裝修合同

溫哥華業主面對獨特情況，書面裝修合同特別重要。屋齡偏高、分層建築管理規則嚴格，加上許可證積壓，承包商預計的工期往往被大幅拉長。根據卑詩省《分層物業法》，涉及公共財產、结构或外觀的裝修必須獲得理事會書面批准。

《卑詩省業主保障法》亦規定，簽署裝修合同並支付押金後，有10天冷靜期。溫哥華裝修糾紛是省內消費者投訴最大類別，10天冷靜期正是為此而設。

計劃廚房、浴室、全屋或商業裝修？免費咨詢聚星裝修，獲取詳細報價。

溫哥華裝修合同必備條款

合法約束力的裝修合同應包括：完整工程範圍說明、詳細價格及付款時間表、含里程碑的工期計劃、工程變更程序（口頭授權不具法律約束力）、責任險及工伤保险证明、保修条款，以及許可證申請責任歸屬。工程的每個細節都應清楚列明。

查看聚星裝修的實際工程範例：素里雙浴室裝修項目。

卑詩省裝修承包商執照要求

根據卑詩省法律，工程造價超過5,000元的承包商必須持有有效卑詩省商業牌照，並向卑詩省房屋局註冊為住宅建築商。持牌建築商必須為其工程提供新房保修保險，包括結構缺陷和材料保證。在卑詩省房屋局網站的《業主保障網上門戶》查證承包商牌照，確認其保險有效。

卑詩省業主押金及付款保障

《卑詩省業主保障法》將押金上限限定為5,000元或合同總價的半數，以較低者為準。工程造價超過1,000元的合同，必須預留至少5%保修金，待工程通過最終驗收後方可發放。聚星裝修按工程進度階段收款，最高預付額不超過5,000元。詳見高貴林廚房裝修項目的付款安排。

爭議解決及自保方法

卑詩省業主可通過《住宅租賃管理局》調解5萬元以下合同糾紛，或通過《卑詩省民事調解法庭》處理5,000元以下申索。預防勝於治療：簽約前確保合同列明爭議解決程序。警惕以下危險信號：拒絕提供詳細工程範圍、要求超過5,000元押金或全額預付款、現金-only安排、無工期計劃、拒絕提供保險證書，以及催促快速簽約。

大溫哥華地區計劃裝修？簽約前先諮詢聚星裝修，我們提供詳細書面報價，不收取任何費用。

常見問題

卑詩省裝修押金上限是多少？

根據《卑詩省業主保障法》，承包商可收取的最高押金為5,000元或合同總價的半數，以較低者為準。若承包商要求更高金額，你有權拒絕並向消費者保障局舉報。

簽約後可以追加工程變更嗎？

可以，但必須經雙方簽署書面工程變更單，確認追加工程的內容及費用，口頭授權不具法律約束力。

如何查證承包商是否持有卑詩省合法牌照？

在卑詩省房屋局網站的《業主保障網上門戶》輸入承包商名稱或註冊編號，查詢其牌照是否有效及保險是否涵蓋當前工程。

卑詩省裝修合同有冷靜期嗎？

有。《卑詩省業主保障法》規定，住宅裝修合同自簽署及支付押金後，有10天冷靜期，期間可無條件取消合同。

房屋保險是否涵蓋裝修工程？

標準房屋保險不涵蓋做工不良或工程未完成的情況，只涵蓋意外及突發性損壞。應確保承包商持有工程材料及工藝保險。
